0.content: Aegis Solutions hires fast, trains little and pays on results. Its crews guard tower lobbies, Cloudridge gates, Dockside yards and Iron Reach plants, and they are known for shooting first and filing reports later. Aegis takes the jobs SDG thinks are beneath it, and the jobs SDG would refuse. It will guard anyone with sol, including people SDG is watching, which is how the two keep colliding. Many Aegis officers are ex-Sentinels who were pushed out, and they brought their old grudges and old contacts with them. Aegis loyalty lasts exactly as long as the contract. When the contract ends, a former client can become a target by morning. Street people find Aegis easier to bribe than SDG and much harder to predict.

1.content: Aegis Solutions is Lowlight's second-largest supplier of armed force, close behind Sentinel Defense Group. SDG sells intelligence and city contracts; Aegis sells protection: guards for the Towers and Cloudridge, escort crews, site security in Dockside and Iron Reach. It is cheaper than SDG and less careful. The two compete for every contract, and now and then their crews meet in the street, and Spectra reports it as an accident. Many Aegis people are ex-SDG, and they do not talk about why they left.

2.content: A booth deck is rented by the hour in a back booth, a curtain and a stool and a deck chained to the table. Second Socket has a row of them; so do half the bars on the Ribbon. It is how people with no deck of their own get on the grid: a kid paying off a debt, a runner whose own deck just died, somebody who needs one job done and no record of owning anything. The catch is that the booth's owner logs every keystroke, and sells the logs to whoever asks nicely. Experienced runners use a booth only for work they don't mind being sold.

3.content: Chiron Medical runs Lowlight's high-end trauma hospitals and the ambulance drones that serve them. The care inside is excellent; getting inside depends on a trauma insurance card. When someone goes down, a drone scans for a card first, and if the card bounces, the drone flies on. People have bled out in the street with a Chiron drone hovering overhead, waiting to confirm. That is where the slang bounced comes from. Most of Lowlight relies on street clinics, back-room doctors and co-ops instead, and Chiron is happy to let them.

4.content: A chrome deck has no box. It is built into the runner, along the forearm or behind the eye, with the keyboard replaced by the nerves that used to drive the hand. It is the fastest way onto the grid and the one thing nobody can take off you at a door. It is also the heaviest chrome a body can carry, and it makes the hum louder than anything else: chrome-deck runners are the first to need the script and the first to go off it badly. Cortex fits them uptown. Ripperdocs fit cheaper ones downstack, and everyone knows which kind lasts.

5.content: Cloudridge sits in the hills on Lowlight's north side. Its mansions line winding roads between the ridges, behind walls, gates and some of the last real trees in the city. It is old money: families who were rich before the corps and stayed rich by marrying into them, investing in them or holding their debts. Cloudridge looks down on the whole city. On clear nights the Velvet cat is plain to see from its terraces, and old Cloudridge families pretend not to notice it. Private security patrols the roads, and anyone on foot is stopped. The newer corporate rich live east in Helios Towers, and Cloudridge looks down on them too.

6.content: Cortex Global's real power on the street is the cart. Cortex doesn't so much sell skills as lease them. Carts are licensed and check in over the grid, so Cortex can update them, throttle them or switch them off. Houses pay Cortex for every carted worker they place, and a worker who leaves their house often finds their carts stop working that week. Cortex keeps the largest private runner force in Lowlight and pays it well, and other runners measure themselves against its lacquer. It buys out small tech shops, hires their best people and closes the rest. Cracked and bootleg carts are its main enemy on the street, and Cortex pays the Capers heavily to hunt the runners who crack them. Cortex rarely uses violence directly. It prefers lawsuits, debt and quiet updates, and it usually gets what it wants.

7.content: Cortex Global is the king of tech in Lowlight: cybernetics, artificial intelligence, and most of the hardware the grid runs on. Its biggest earner is the skill-chip implant, the cart, which lets a worker run a skill they never learned, from welding to surgery to a new language. Houses buy carts in bulk for the people they place, and many workers are carted before they are hired. Cortex says carts are safe. Long-term users mention headaches, lost time, and the strange feeling that their hands know things they do not. Cortex is said to pay its runners best in the city, and its lacquer is the thickest on the grid.

8.content: The Cortex Meridian is the deck the corps issue and the one ordinary people can buy legally: a beige slab with a good keyboard, fast, reliable, and licensed. Like a cart, a Meridian checks in over the grid. Cortex can update it, throttle it, or switch it off, and it knows where every one of them is. Runners call it the leash. A corp runner on a Meridian is the fastest thing on the grid, and the easiest to find. Street runners won't touch a clean one, and a runner who shows up with one is either new, stupid, or working for someone they shouldn't be.

9.content: Cortex Relay is the phone network almost everyone in Lowlight uses. It is a Cortex Global subsidiary, cheap enough that the Houses hand out Relay decks with a placement, and its towers cover every district except the deepest Hollows and the drowned blocks of the Marsh. Everyone knows the Relay keeps every text and sells what it reads. Corp security buys it by the district, Spectra buys it for stories, and a fixer can buy one person's week for the price of a good dinner. So people text the Relay as if someone is reading: plain talk, nothing about work, no names that matter. Anything that does matter goes in person, through a burner bought that morning, or "on copper": paid to the Copper-Heads and carried on the old Karasu lines, which the Relay cannot see.

10.content: A deck is how a runner gets on the grid: a heavy keyboard unit with cartridge slots, a screen of amber or green text, and a cable to the jack behind the ear. Decks differ in four ways runners care about: how fast they run, how many carts and programs they hold, how hot they are (how easily the deck leads back to whoever is using it), and, for chrome decks, how loud they make the hum. Corp decks are fast and traceable; street decks are slow, cheap and quiet; the rare ones are rare for a reason. New decks come from Cortex dealers uptown. Everything else comes from the Ribbon: Second Socket's counter and the room behind it, repair stalls downstack, and people who don't give their names. Nobody admits to owning more than one.

11.content: Dead Air is a network of pirate broadcasters who cut into Spectra's feeds and replace them with the truth, or their version of it. A screen on the Ribbon flickers, the Spectra anchor vanishes, and for a minute or two Dead Air plays footage the city was never meant to see, often supplied by True-North. Then the feed snaps back and Spectra pretends nothing happened. Dead Air also runs illegal radio stations with music, news and call-in shows, and the stations move every few nights. Its members are a mix of activists, artists and runners, and nobody knows the full roster. Spectra and SDG hunt them constantly. Ordinary people love them and quote them, and would never admit it on the grid.

12.content: A deaf Meridian is a Cortex deck with its check-in chip pulled, so it no longer reports to Cortex. It is nearly as fast as a clean one and far cheaper, because most of them are stolen. Second Socket sells them under the counter and doesn't ask. The catch is the serial number, etched into the board where it can't be filed off without killing the deck. If a Caper or Cortex ever reads it, the person holding it is the person who bought a stolen leash. Runners use one for a year or two, then sell it on before it gets famous.

13.content: Between Pylon Forty and its neighbours, in the shadow of the deck, the Spine holds a night market that never quite closes. Stalls go up under patched tarps on strings of bulbs and paper lanterns: woks and skewers and cheap dumplings, a glass-repair booth that will fix an implant without asking where it came from, a pirate radio stall playing whatever got past the filters, second-hand jackets, a small shrine with candles in red glass. It's loud, crowded and cheap, and the freight overhead drowns half of every conversation. Spiners come to eat, trade and be seen. People who are being followed come because it is the easiest place on the Spine to stop being followed. Sentinels walk through only during a tide, and the market is always half-packed by the time they arrive.

14.content: A dock slate is a Voltaic Logistics freight terminal: a ruggedised grey deck with a rubber keyboard, built to be dropped off cranes and rained on. Thousands of them work the docks and the Spine, and they go missing all the time. Out of the box a slate only reads manifests. Cracked, it is a cheap, ugly, nearly unbreakable starter deck, slow and short on slots, and nobody looks twice at a dock worker carrying one. Most runners in the Strand and Dockside started on a slate, and some never saw a reason to stop.

15.content: Dockside lies across Lowlight Bay from Karasu, between the water and Iron Reach. It is the city's freight port: miles of stacked containers, piers and warehouses, with the big red cranes working through the night, nearly all of them Voltaic's. Most of the loading is automated now. The human crews that remain are hard, underpaid and protective of their jobs. The container stacks form a maze that changes every day, and plenty goes missing in it, some of it on purpose. Anyone who needs cargo moved quietly into or out of Lowlight ends up dealing with someone in Dockside.

16.content: Drownworks, south of the Marsh, is the part of the lower city that was saved before it sank. It is home to Lowlight's water reclamation: huge glowing settling bays, filtration halls, pump houses, and pipes running in every direction. It looks like heavy, dirty industry and the work is hard, but the water that comes out of Drownworks is as pure as water gets, and the people who make it are proud of that. They call the district the Works and themselves Works people. The slang clean water, meaning honest or reliable, is theirs. Works crews keep their word, look after their own, and take it personally when anyone threatens the water.

17.content: Fairy Dust is the loudest band on the Ribbon: four players from downstack who play glitter-punk, fast and sloppy, with cheap synths run through broken amps and a singer called Moth who screams half the words and sings the rest. They play the clubs on Level 5 and any room that will have them, and their shows end with the crowd covered in cheap glitter that turns up in everyone's hair for a week. Spectra won't play them since a song called "Spectra Says" called the network a liar by name, so their music lives on bootleg chips, in shop speakers and on Dead Air's pirate radio, which plays them often. Their shirts are everywhere downstack, mostly fakes, and the band says fakes are fine. Nobody upstack admits to liking them. Everybody downstack knows the words.

18.content: A companion house in Velvet, Lowlight's red-light quarter: discreet and expensive. A house places its workers and holds their payout, which is how it keeps them. Nix Neon worked out of Glass Orchid for nine years before she left. Leaving is possible, and the house remembers. Its Host is Vesna Halloran, who keeps the floor all night at the long bar under the paper lanterns. Whether she owns the house or fronts for someone who does is anyone's guess.

19.content: Words from the grid and the chrome trade. Lacquer is corp security on the grid, the layered defenses wrapped around anything worth taking; thick lacquer kills. The dark is the unlisted back half of the grid, where runners meet and nothing is indexed. Carts are skill-chip implants, named for the cartridge they slot in like. A carted worker runs a skill they never learned, and borrowed hands is the polite word for them. The hum is the noise chrome makes in the mind before the mind breaks; the corps call it cyber-psychosis. The script is the MiraGen subscription that keeps the hum down, and people who miss a payment are off script. A ghost is a runner nobody has ever seen in person, which describes most of the good ones.

20.content: Hae's Noodles is a street stall on Level 4 of the Ribbon, directly under Lowlight Intake: a deep wooden counter, a handful of worn stools, a striped dark-red awning with paper lanterns under it, and a red neon bowl-and-chopsticks sign with no words on it, because everyone on the level knows what it is. An old vending machine hums beside it. The stockpot is never off. Hae serves one broth and two noodles, with whatever topping was cheap at the market that morning. Like most food on the Ribbon, it's mostly Soma, but the broth is her own, and it tastes like it. She takes hard sol, runs a tab for people she trusts, and doesn't discuss either. Hae says little and notices everything, and she doesn't gossip about anyone who eats at her counter. Regulars don't order; she already knows. Half the Intake's clients eat here before they go up the stairs, and some never go up at all, and she lets them sit as long as they need. When the late ones come down from upstairs, a second bowl is already out.

21.content: Halloran, P.I. is the detective holovid everybody in Lowlight has seen at least once: a tired private eye in a long coat who works cases in the rain, owes money to the wrong people, and never trusts what Spectra says. It has run on and off for decades with different actors in the coat. People who care argue that the early seasons are the real ones, before Spectra bought the show and made Halloran friendlier with the Sentinels. The old episodes trade on paper-chips, and some of them don't match the versions Spectra streams now. Fans quote its lines in bars, and "Halloran it" means to work out who did something by asking around instead of looking it up on the grid.

22.content: Helios Towers, called the Towers, is where Lowlight's corporate elite live, east of Cloudridge. There are only five towers, but each one is effectively its own city, with its own housing, schools, clinics, shops, security and rules. Each is governed separately, and city law applies inside only as far as each tower allows. Residents can go years without touching the ground. Workers from below come in through service entrances, are scanned on the way in and out, and are not allowed above certain floors. From the street, the Towers look like the future Lowlight was promised. From inside, the city below looks like weather.

23.content: Lowlight was founded in 1878 as Karasu, a harbor settlement on the bay. The old name survives in its oldest district. The city grew outward from the harbor in rings of brick, then concrete, then glass. In the late 1900s the sea started coming in. The city raised the Spine to carry its roads over the water and save the ground that was left, and from then on it built up instead of out. The Marsh went under anyway. In the 2050s fuel costs ended most space flight. The companies that had bet on orbit, Titan above all, came home poorer and meaner. The age of the corps followed. Nexus became the real seat of power, and the Shelf became a place where laws are signed rather than made. Lowlight does not teach its own history. Spectra changes the story every few years. The oldest people in Karasu still tell it the way it happened.

24.content: Iron Reach is Lowlight's industrial zone. It holds every kind of heavy industry except water reclamation, which is just as well, because it is the last place anyone would want to get water. Foundries, refineries, chemical plants and assembly halls run day and night, and the stacks never stop smoking. The air tastes of metal. Workers live in company blocks between the plants, get paid through houses, and wear out their lungs young. The northeast end is different: newer, cleaner plants that build chrome, decks and parts for the Nexus corps, with better pay, tighter security and fewer windows. People from the old Reach say the high-tech end is still Iron Reach, it just washes its hands more.

25.content: Kalimera Bay is a sunbaked harbour town across the water, old white stone stacked up a hillside above a bay that keeps getting higher. The sea has already taken its lower streets, the way it took the Marsh, and the fishing that kept it alive has thinned to almost nothing. Its people leave by boat, whole families at once, and arrive on Tidal Isle with a little money, a lot of relatives and very few papers. Kalimerans in Lowlight run small kitchens, mend boats and nets, and drift toward the Marsh and the Strand, anywhere near water. They are warm, loud and slow to trust officials of any kind. The name means good morning, and they still say it to each other at any hour.

26.content: Karaköy Deep is a sea-gate city across the water, built on both banks of a deep strait that half the sea's shipping has to pass through. Its ferries run all night, its pilots know every current, and its docks have always been friendly to cargo that doesn't want to be counted. That reputation follows its people: customs on Tidal Isle look twice at anyone from the Deep, and the Ferrymen are said to hire its pilots for their night boats. Karaköy people in Lowlight work the water, the freight yards and the markets, trade in everything and keep their word once they have given it. They call the strait the Deep, and Lowlight has picked up the habit.

27.content: Karasu is Lowlight's oldest district. It was the whole city when it was founded in 1878, under that name. It has two neighborhoods: Old Town, the habs, most of them abandoned, and the Ribbon, the stacked road that grows out of the restored part of Old Town and winds down toward the Strand. Karasu's bones are older than anything else in the city: brick under concrete, iron under chrome, streets laid out for carts and never widened. Reconstruction has rebuilt pockets of it to look modern, but every new front is bolted to an old wall. The rest of Lowlight treats Karasu like an old relative, with respect, some embarrassment, and no plans to visit.

28.content: Lowlight Intake is a sliding-scale counseling co-op in one room above Hae's Noodles on Level 4 of the Ribbon, up a flight of stairs off the street. It runs nights, 20:00 to 04:00, and Nix is its night counselor. Clients pay what they can, and the fee still has to clear. It sees ex-workers, Ribbon staff, dock burnouts, blanks and off-script chrome, and it refers out anything that needs a doctor. Like every co-op, it keeps its notes on paper, initials only, and it does not tell SDG who came through the door; the sign on the door says as much. The room does several jobs at once: a desk with three old screens and a lamp, a kitchenette with a kettle, a tall shelf of binders and files, and a daybed under a big window onto the Ribbon where people can sit, or sleep if they need to. Pipes and conduit run across every wall, the building is never fully quiet, and the smell of Hae's broth comes up through the floor all night.

29.content: Common street words, used without explanation. Blanks are people with no record on the grid, most of them squatting in Old Town. Bounced means left to die because your trauma card did not clear. Clean water means honest or reliable: she's clean water. Drowned means gone under, ruined or vanished. The Cat's up means night has started. Upstack and downstack mean higher or lower on the Ribbon, and by extension richer or poorer. Spectra says means probably false. Under the Wheel means out on the Strand. The tide is a corp security sweep; when the tide's in, people stay home. Like all Lowlight slang, these words are not used by people who have not earned them.

30.content: Lowlight behaves like someone who has been cheated too many times. It is patient, watchful and never generous. Everything in it is for rent: light, water, air on the upper levels, a clean record, a few hours of being left alone. Darkness is the only free thing, and most people live in it. Neon covers the whole city now, but it belongs to whoever pays for it, and it only shows you what someone wants to sell. The city remembers debts and forgets people. The corps own the streets and the grid. Runners move through the grid unseen. Ordinary people keep their heads down and their business on paper. Public violence is rare, and it is common everywhere else. Nobody calls Lowlight beautiful out loud, but people who leave talk about it for the rest of their lives. The tech is old and patched: humming screens, heavy keys, cables, cartridges, things repaired instead of replaced. The only new thing in Lowlight is the money.

31.content: Mirage Heights, called the Shelf, sits on the cliffs at the city's northeast edge, above Velvet. It holds Lowlight's government: council chambers, ministries, courts, and the homes of the officials who staff them, all in a guarded enclave with a view over the whole bay. Officially the Shelf governs Lowlight. In practice it signs what Nexus drafts and enforces it with security rented from SDG. Its officials are comfortable and well paid, and few of them have been down to the Ribbon in years. When something is decided on the Shelf, Lowlight assumes it was decided somewhere else first.

32.content: MiraGen's power is the script. Hundreds of thousands of chromed people in Lowlight need its monthly edits to keep the hum away, and MiraGen sets the price, the renewal date and the terms. Prices rise without warning, and accounts are suspended over billing errors. Subscribers who fall behind are offered payment plans that bind them to a house or a corp contract. MiraGen also supplies combat drugs to SDG and Aegis, and it tests new compounds in clinics in the poorer districts, paying volunteers in script. Its biggest threat is the Lazarus Net, and MiraGen spends heavily to find the Net's sellers and frighten its buyers. MiraGen likes to be seen as the company keeping Lowlight sane. The people on the script see it as the company keeping them on a leash.

33.content: MiraGen Pharmaceuticals makes combat drugs for SDG and Aegis, neural boosters for students and runners, and the gene-therapy edits that keep heavy chrome users from going into the hum, which the corps call cyber-psychosis. The edits are not a cure but a subscription, renewed monthly at a steep price, and Lowlight calls it the script. Anyone with enough chrome is on the script or knows they should be. Going off script means missing a payment, and people off script are avoided on sight. MiraGen says the subscription funds research. Everyone else says MiraGen found a way to rent out sanity.

34.content: Mother Rot is the Marsh's fence and moneylender: a big, warm, gold-hung man in a damp olive suit, with an old amber glass where his left eye was and a real cigar in his hand. Nobody knows his real name, and he tells the story of the name differently every time. He works out of the Counting House, the top floors of a drowned bank whose lobby is a lagoon; visitors come by boat. Sump-Rat salvage goes through him to shops on the Ribbon and warehouses in Dockside, and he pays fairly and on time. He lends hard sol to people the grid won't touch and would rather be paid in favors. Once a week anyone can eat broth on his roof. A debtor who won't pay loses the boat, then the roof, then everyone's goodwill; he calls it letting the water have them. Everyone argues about what is in the bank's flooded vault.

35.content: The Neon Strand, the Strand to everyone, is where the Ribbon comes down and levels out at the water. It is Lowlight's entertainment district and the first part of the city to go fully neon; the rest of Lowlight copied it. The fairgrounds sit on the boardwalk over the bay: rides, games, arcades, food carts and shooting galleries, all a little older and more dangerous than they look. Families come in the early evening, and after the Cat's up, the crowd changes. The Strand sells the feeling of a good time to people who cannot afford a real one. Pickpockets, dealers and recruiters for the houses work the boardwalk every night, and corp security leaves them alone as long as the lights stay on.

36.content: Nexus is Lowlight's core. The most powerful corps keep their headquarters here, and this is where the city is actually run. Its towers are the brightest in Lowlight, wrapped in moving signs and logos, and the streets between them are clean, patrolled and full of people walking fast. Cortex Global, Sentinel Defense Group, Soma, MiraGen, Chiron, Voltaic, Titan and Spectra all have their seats here, alongside dozens of smaller corps hoping to join them. The banks that back the sol are here too. The Shelf passes the laws, but Nexus drafts them. Ordinary people come to Nexus to work, apply, appeal or be judged, and they leave as soon as they can.

37.content: Nix's walk-up is one room up four flights of stairs with no lift, in a block on the Ribbon a short walk from the Intake. It is hers, not a workplace: she doesn't see clients here, and almost nobody else comes up. A folding paper screen painted with cherry branches hides the bed, and the curtains over the one window stay shut, because she works nights and sleeps through most of the day. There is a kitchenette she rarely cooks in, a small table usually covered in takeout cartons and empty cans, plants that somehow survive, prints of skylines and moons on the walls, and clothes on the floor. Her desk is crowded with old screens she keeps running long after newer hardware would be cheaper, and what she won't put on the grid sits beside them in paper folders. The room is lived in rather than kept, warm and quiet, and it is the one place in Lowlight where nobody needs anything from her.

38.content: Oksana's is a counter at the foot of Pylon Forty, cut into the concrete where a maintenance bay used to be, open to the street under the Spine's deck behind a roll-up steel shutter. Six stools, a zinc counter worn bright where elbows go, a steel urn of black tea that is never empty, tea served in glasses in tin holders, and one dish worth crossing the Spine for: dumplings, boiled or fried, with whatever filling was cheap, sour cream if you ask, dill whether you ask or not. An old radio plays the freight report and talk shows nobody listens to. When a heavy hauler crosses the joint overhead, the glasses walk an inch along the counter, and the regulars put out a hand without looking. Oksana runs it alone. She feeds the night-shift lift crews before they start, keeps a tab for the hangers, and never asks anyone what they do. Spiners say nothing said at her counter reaches the street, and that she knows who's missing before their families do.

39.content: Old Karasu decks were built before the corps lacquered the grid: wooden or brass cases, valve-warm amber text, keyboards that clack like typewriters. They are slow, they hold almost nothing, and they speak protocols the modern grid was built on and the lacquer never quite closed. A runner on one can find ghost doors, ways into corp systems that no modern deck can see because nothing modern knows to look. Runners say there are three left in the city, and nobody agrees on who has them. Every few years someone claims to own one, and every few years someone stops talking about it.

40.content: Old Town is Karasu's residential half, block after block of old habs. About three quarters of it is officially abandoned: no power on the meters, no names on the leases, windows bricked up or open to the rain. People live there anyway. They are the unknowns, blanks with no record on the grid, and they keep it that way. Lights move in buildings that have been dark for decades, and strangers who walk in without a reason do not always walk out. The rest of Old Town is reconstruction, blocks rebuilt with city money and corp grants, new skins on old frames. Those buildings look almost modern, and the people in them pay rent. At night they hear the dead blocks next door: water in the pipes, footsteps on stairs nobody should be using. The Ribbon starts in the reconstructed part and climbs from there.

41.content: A pocket deck has no keyboard, only a thumb pad and a strip of screen, and it is small enough to tape inside a jacket or under a sleeve. It holds one or two carts and runs slow, and no runner would choose it for real work on the grid. It is the deck for walking into places: guards check bags and cuffs, not seams, and a pocket deck can open a door, wipe a camera loop, or pass a file in the time it takes someone to look away. Runners on a slip carry one. Owning one is not illegal; owning one with a door program on it is.

42.content: Pylon Forty is one of the Spine's great concrete legs, where the highway passes between Nexus and Karasu on its long run south toward the Marsh. Like most pylons it is a building now. Hab rings are cut into the concrete around the old maintenance lift, nine floors of them, and the higher you live, the closer you are to the road. The top ring sits right under the deck, where every heavy hauler hits an expansion joint with a sound like a door slamming, all night. Below the deck, between Forty and Forty-One, the hangers hang: habs built out of shipping steel and slung from the deck girders on cables, reached by a cable stair that sways when you use it. Their floors are grating, and under the grating is a long way down. At the foot of the pylon, open to the street under the deck, Oksana's counter keeps the lights on. A lift-maintenance office on the second ring has a company name on the door and nobody who ever fixes the lift. Spiners in Forty say you stop hearing the freight after a month, and you start hearing it again the night something is wrong.

43.content: The Quantum Detainment Facility, the QDF, is Lowlight's great prison, a hard dark mass on the northwest corner of Tidal Isle. Officially it holds the city's most dangerous offenders. Unofficially it holds anyone the corps or the Shelf want gone. Nobody outside agrees on what the quantum in its name means, and the people who might know do not talk. Everyone does know that it holds more prisoners than it seems to have room for, that visits are rarely granted, and that the few people who come out stay quiet afterward. Locals call it the Q. Nobody jokes about it twice.

44.content: Scoma is the cartel behind the knockoff stims flooding the Ribbon and the Strand. The name is short for Soma scams: cheap copies of Soma's designer stims, cooked in Iron Reach and the Marsh, packaged to look like the real thing, and sold for a fraction of the price. Some batches are nearly as good as Soma's, and some kill. Scoma dealers work the boardwalk under Wheel-Men protection and the lower Ribbon on their own, and Scoma pays the Freight Runners to bring precursors in through Dockside. Soma condemns Scoma in public and tolerates it in private, since the knockoffs keep demand high and make the real product look safe. Scoma's bosses are businesspeople, not street fighters, and they settle disputes with price wars before they settle them with guns.

45.content: SDG's headquarters is the Sentinel Tower in Nexus, a dark glass column with no logo on it, because everyone already knows. The public sees the lobby: grey stone, a scanner arch, and a desk where people who have been called in wait to be told why. The sixty-first floor has no number on the lift panel. It is the branch's floor. Carpet that swallows footsteps, glass walls between the offices, real wood on the desks, a coffee machine that costs more than a year in a Spine hab, and windows from floor to ceiling. Rain runs down them most nights, and the city below looks like weather. Nothing on the floor is loud. Nobody raises their voice, nobody runs, and nobody looks at another officer's screen. Case officers come up when they are called and go back down when they are done. It is the cleanest room most of them will ever stand in, and none of them stay longer than they have to.

46.comment: Sentinel Defense Group on the street
46.content: On the street, SDG is the law, and it behaves like a business that sells it. Sentinels patrol Nexus, the Shelf, the Towers' service levels and anywhere else a client pays for coverage. Districts that don't pay only see them during a tide. Response time depends on who called. SDG keeps files on everyone who matters and plenty who don't, and it trades in favors as much as sol: a Sentinel can make a charge disappear, or appear. Its plainclothes branch, which officially has no name, runs informants on every level of the Ribbon. When it catches runners, it would rather buy them than jail them. SDG avoids open fights with gangs. It prefers to let them bleed each other and then arrest the survivors. Its rivalry with Aegis is the city's worst-kept secret. Crossing a single Sentinel is survivable. Crossing SDG as a company is not, and the people who try it end up in the Q.

47.content: Sentinel Defense Group, SDG, is a private intelligence corp and Lowlight's main supplier of armed force. When the city needs police, guards, riot lines or soldiers, it rents them from SDG. Its agents watch the grid, the streets and the other corps, and SDG sells what it learns to the highest bidder. Its uniformed people are called Sentinels. Its plainclothes people are not called anything, because nobody is sure who they are. When the tide comes in, SDG is usually behind it. Aegis Solutions is its closest rival.

48.content: A Sentinel field deck is SDG hardware: an armoured, single-purpose unit built for breaking into things, with an ICE breaker wired into the board instead of loaded from a cart. It does one job and does it better than anything sold in Lowlight. Owning one is illegal for anyone outside Sentinel, and they turn up on the street only when one goes missing from a depot or off a body. SDG counts them. When one surfaces anywhere, SDG comes looking for where it went, and it doesn't stop at the person who was holding it.

49.content: Skarnholm is a cold freeport across the water, kept dry by dykes and lit by the wind farms along its coast. It is rich, orderly and closed, and the people who leave it are rarely poor. More often they are running from a debt, a contract or a corp they signed their life to. Skarnholmers who come through the Ferrymen tend to arrive with a corp sponsor's name on their papers and a good reason not to use it. In Lowlight they are quiet, precise and hard to read. Corps hire them as engineers and managers, and the Houses value them as staff who never make a scene. They find Lowlight loud and warm, and most never go back.

50.content: Local words, used plainly: glass for an ocular implant; the grid for the network; a house for an agency that places workers and holds their pay; chrome for hardware in a body; paper for anything you refuse to put on a server; the Ribbon for the strip. People don't use slang they haven't earned.

51.content: The sol is Lowlight's currency. The name is short for solutions per second, the measure of mining speed the money was first pegged to. Its value still rides on how much computing the city's banks can prove. The word is the same in singular and plural: one sol, a billion sol. Most sol moves as numbers on the grid, through accounts the corps can see. Hard sol, meaning printed scrip and coin, still circulates in Karasu, the Marsh and Velvet, and anyone who pays in hard sol is assumed to have a reason. Being broke is being sol-sick. Prices rise with altitude. The same bowl of noodles costs more on the upper Ribbon than the lower, and more again on the Shelf, if anyone there ate noodles.

52.content: Soma is the biotech giant behind three things almost everyone in Lowlight touches. For the rich, it grows cloned organs, so a Cloudridge heart can be replaced as often as needed. For the night life, it makes designer stims, sold legally on the upper Ribbon and illegally everywhere else. For everyone, it makes the synthetic food that feeds the city: paste, protein, noodles and flavor packs. Real food is a luxury. When Soma has a bad quarter, the food gets worse, and people notice before the news does.

53.comment: Spectra Broadcast Network on the street
53.content: Spectra rules by narrative. Its Nexus newsrooms take commissions from corporate boards, the Shelf and anyone else who can pay, so the story of the day is whatever was bought that morning. Its archive division rewrites old broadcasts, and its runners hunt down surviving copies of the originals. Spectra's anchors are celebrities, and its street crews film anything violent enough to sell. Spectra can make a person famous, guilty or forgotten overnight. Its two great enemies are True-North, who preserve the originals, and Dead Air, who jam its feeds; on air, Spectra calls both of them terrorists. Most people in Lowlight don't believe Spectra, but they watch it anyway, and whatever Spectra says becomes the official record whether anyone believes it or not.

54.content: Spectra Broadcast Network, SBN or just Spectra, is Lowlight's news conglomerate. It owns most of the channels, feeds and screens in the city, and every day it tells Lowlight what happened, in whatever version the highest-paying corporate board wants. Spectra does more than spin the news. It rewrites the past: events change, people are added or removed, and old broadcasts are quietly replaced. Spectra says means probably false. People who want the truth ask the old people, check paper, or pay a runner to find the original files before Spectra overwrites them.

55.content: A stall build is a deck put together downstack at a repair stall out of whatever came through: a salvaged board, mismatched keycaps, a screen from something else, extra cart slots soldered in where there was never meant to be room. Every one is different. The good ones beat a Meridian for slots and cost a quarter of the price, carry no serial anyone can trace, and run hot enough to burn a hand. They also die at bad moments. Runners say a stall build is only as good as the stall, and the stalls downstack on the Ribbon are where the good ones come from.

56.content: Sundarpur is a vast monsoon delta city across the water, crowded, humid and half flooded every rainy season. It has more back-street clinics than anywhere else on the sea, and its cut-price chrome work and copied MiraGen script travel everywhere, which is why Lowlight's customs check Sundarpuri arrivals for medical papers more often than most. Sundarpuris come to Lowlight as clinic hands, technicians, nurses and cooks, often with real skills and no paperwork that proves them. Many end up working for the co-ops or the street clinics, where nobody asks for a licence. They are quick, practical and patient with bureaucracy, having grown up with plenty of it.

57.content: Everyone in Lowlight knows SDG has people who don't wear the grey, and almost nobody can say who they are. The street calls them plainclothes, or case officers when it wants to sound like it knows more. What the street believes: they don't arrest good runners, they buy them, with a charge that goes away as long as you keep working, and comes back the day you stop. They pay well and on time. They sit next to you at a counter for weeks before they say what they want, and some of them are kind about it, which people say is worse. Their glass is better than anything sold on the Ribbon, and the rumour is that it records. Runners warn each other about a stranger who buys tea too often. Nobody can prove any of it, and the people who could have a reason not to.

58.content: The Breakers rule the habs beneath the Spine. They began as a crew that broke into maintenance shafts and service decks, and they now control the inside of the highway: its stairwells, cable tunnels, and the hidden routes between pylons. They tax anything that moves through their territory, tap power from the Spine's lighting lines, and sell freight that falls, or is pushed, from the decks above. Breakers mark territory by smashing the lights; when a stretch under the Spine goes dark, it belongs to them. They are loud, young and violent, and their fights sometimes spill up onto the Spine itself. The Spiners who live alongside them pay their dues and keep their doors locked.

59.content: The Capers are runners who hunt runners. They work for whoever pays: Cortex, Spectra, MiraGen, SDG, the Shelf. They trace intrusions to their source, burn decks remotely, and sell names and locations to the people who want them. Capers are well paid and well protected. Many were once Strip-Miners, or worse, who got caught and were offered a choice. The rest of the runner world despises them. Capers rarely make the physical arrest themselves; they find the person, and SDG or Aegis does the rest. Runners say the name is a joke about the jobs they ruin, and every runner in Lowlight has a story about one.

60.content: Along the outside edge of the Spine's deck, a narrow steel maintenance catwalk runs between the pylons, meant for crews who stopped coming years ago. Near Pylon Forty you can reach it through a service hatch off the top ring, or by climbing out past the hung habs, and both are trespass. The traffic roars past on the other side of the crash barrier, close enough to shake the grating, and on the open side there is only a waist-high rail and the whole city below: the core's towers, the Ribbon stacked up in light, the bay and its ship lights, the highway curving away on its legs. A sodium lamp leans out over the edge and a yellow warning beacon nobody switches off turns slowly at the end. Spiners go out there to smoke, to think, to be alone, or to be alone with someone. Nobody official ever comes, and nobody falls, mostly.

61.content: The co-ops are Lowlight's mutual aid network: sliding-scale clinics, counseling offices, food kitchens, legal help and shelters, run by volunteers and paid for with whatever comes in. Lowlight Intake on the Ribbon is one of them. The co-ops are the only safety net most people in the city have, and they serve anyone who walks in, from blanks to bounced workers to off-script chrome. They keep their records on paper and off the grid, and they will not tell SDG who came through the door. They have no weapons and little money, but they have many quiet friends: the Waterkeepers, the Copper-Heads, Dead Air, and plenty of people who once needed help themselves. The corps find them inconvenient. The gangs mostly leave them alone, because sooner or later everyone needs a co-op.

62.content: The Copper-Heads are old-school runners who work through the city's original copper phone and data lines, laid in Karasu more than a century ago and forgotten by everyone else. Their gear is analog and handmade: patched decks, line taps, switch boxes hidden in Old Town walls. The copper network barely registers on the modern grid, so corp security almost never sees it, and the Copper-Heads use it to move messages, money and data where nobody can watch. Many of them live among the Hollows. They tend to be older than other runners, suspicious of new tech and contemptuous of carts. They charge more than anyone to move a message, and they lose fewer.

63.content: The Drowned Choir is a cult in the Marsh that believes the sea is judgment. It teaches that Lowlight was condemned for its greed, that the Marsh was only the first to fall, and that the water will keep rising until it takes Nexus, the Towers and the Shelf. Members gather on rooftops and in half-flooded halls to sing at the waterline, and they baptize converts in the canals. As far as anyone can prove, they are not violent, but people who wrong them have a habit of drowning, and Choir members talk about it calmly. The Choir takes in the desperate and gives them food and purpose, which makes it popular in the Marsh and spreading into the Spine. The Sump-Rats trade with them and keep their distance.

64.content: The Ferrymen get people into Lowlight through Tidal Isle. They forge papers, bribe customs officers, hide people in cargo, and run them off the Isle by boat at night. Their price is high and few can pay it up front, so most clients pay in labor, owed for years to a house the Ferrymen choose. Some never finish paying. The Ferrymen also get people out of the holding blocks, and sometimes out of Lowlight entirely, for anyone with enough sol. They have officers inside customs and boats on the bay, and they work with the Freight Runners and the Sump-Rats. They are polite and punctual, and they show no mercy at all to anyone who tries to skip a debt.

65.content: The Freight Runners are Dockside's smugglers and thieves. They work the gaps in Voltaic's automation: the minutes between a crane setting a container down and a scanner reading it, the stacks the cameras can't see, the manifests a friendly runner can edit. Many are dock workers, or the children of dock workers Voltaic laid off, and they think of theft as back pay. They move contraband into the city, lift cargo out of it, and rent container space to anyone who needs to hide something, or someone. Voltaic tolerates them up to a point. The Freight Runners know exactly where that point is and stay just under it, and they deal with anyone who pushes past it themselves, before Aegis has to.

66.content: The grid is Lowlight's network, and almost everything that matters happens there first. It looks old: amber and green text, scan lines, sound through cheap speakers. Runners connect through decks, which are heavy keyboard units with cartridge slots and a cable to a jack behind the ear. They do the work nobody admits to paying for: moving money, erasing records, stealing designs, burying stories before Spectra can run them. Every corp employs runners and every corp hunts them. Most people never know a runner has touched their life. They only know that a debt vanished, a file appeared, or a door stopped opening. Ordinary people treat the grid like weather. They use it but do not trust it, and anything they cannot afford to lose goes on paper.

67.content: The Hollows are the blanks who hold Old Town's abandoned blocks. They are less a gang than a community with teeth: unregistered people, runaways, deserters and others the grid forgot, living in buildings the city wrote off. They guard the dead blocks against strangers, scavengers, SDG and reconstruction crews, and they have rigged the buildings with traps, false floors and blocked stairwells. Inside, they keep their own rules and their own peace. They distrust anyone with a grid record, which is almost everyone. Some Copper-Heads live among them and keep their lines running. The Hollows will sometimes trade with or help an outsider, but only through go-betweens, and never twice by the same route.

68.content: The houses are the placement agencies that hire out most of Lowlight's workers, and together they are one of the city's great powers. A house finds you work, buys your carts, negotiates your contract and holds your pay, releasing it on its own schedule after taking its cut. Leaving a house is legal and very hard: debts come due, carts stop working, and no other house will take you. The big houses work for the corps, placing labor in Iron Reach, Dockside and the Towers. Smaller houses run Velvet, the Strand and the Ribbon. The houses compete fiercely with each other but close ranks against anything that threatens the system itself. To a worker, their house is family, landlord, bank and jailer all at once.

69.content: The Lazarus Net is an online black market for pirated script, the MiraGen edits that keep the hum away. It lives in the dark, changes location constantly, and takes payment in untraceable sol. Buyers get a cracked edit file and the address of a back-room clinic willing to apply it. Quality varies: some edits are perfect copies, some fail within weeks, and some are poison. Even so, for thousands of chromed people priced off script, the Net is all that stands between them and the hum. Nobody knows who runs it, and its sellers rotate. MiraGen calls it murder and pays the Capers to hunt it. The people it keeps alive call it the only mercy in Lowlight.

70.content: The Long Haul is a hauler stop built into a Spine pylon at deck level, a little north of Pylon Forty, reached by a service ramp that drivers use and nobody else is supposed to. It has been open all night for as long as anyone on the Spine remembers. A long counter with chrome stools, a flat-top griddle, two coffee urns that are never empty, a pie case nobody trusts, an old jukebox, and a row of oxblood booths along wide windows onto the deck, where the heavy haulers park with their marker lights on and the traffic goes by close enough to feel. A pink neon cup glows in the window. The drivers who eat there come off twelve-hour shifts and don't care who's in the next booth, which is why people who need somewhere ordinary to sit with someone go there. The coffee is bad, the eggs are real, and the corner booth at the far end is the one couples and deals both end up in.

71.content: The Low Roller is the giant ferris wheel on the Strand's boardwalk. It is large enough to see from almost anywhere in Lowlight, its ring of lights turning slowly over the bay. Everyone calls it the Wheel. Its cars hold small parties, and some are rented by the hour for meetings nobody wants overheard, since a car at the top is the only private room on the Strand. People use the Wheel to find their way home and to tell which way they are facing. When it stops turning, which has happened only a few times, the whole city notices.

72.content: The Marsh is the part of Lowlight that went under. It lies east of the Strand and sank below the waterline as the sea came in, so its streets are now canals and its lower floors are flooded. The city tried to save it more than once. Billions of sol went into pumps, seawalls and restoration plans, every effort failed, and finally the money stopped. People still live on the upper floors and the roofs. They move by boat and plank bridge, fish from windows, and trade in whatever floats in. The Marsh is poor, damp and mostly ungoverned. The corps ignore it unless something worth taking surfaces. The slang word drowned comes from here.

73.content: The OhhCee's, short for the overclocked, are heavily chromed people who went off script and decided not to come back. Some couldn't afford MiraGen's subscription; others refused it. They push their chrome past its limits and treat the hum as a high, a faith and a warning to everyone else. They are fast, strong and unpredictable, and they burn out young, so the membership is always changing. They hold no territory, only whatever place they are drinking or fighting in that night, usually on the lower Ribbon or the Strand. Other gangs hire them as shock troops and regret it. Ordinary people cross the street when they see one coming. MiraGen points to them as proof of what happens without the script, and Spectra puts them on the news whenever renewals come due.

74.content: A ripperdoc low on the Ribbon, in an old repair shop behind a steel shutter that never goes all the way up. There is no name on it, only a red neon open hand in the door's window, and that is what everyone calls it. Inside: one surgical chair with the straps left hanging, a ring lamp on a jointed arm, a cabinet of second-hand chrome (hands, eyes, spinal plates, coils of neural cable, most of it out of somebody else) and a fridge of MiraGen script sold at a markup to people who are a week from being off script. It is what Karasu gets instead of Chiron: nobody checks your card, the work is good, and nobody asks where the parts came from. It is clean around the chair and nowhere else, and it never closes all the way either.

75.content: The Ribbon began as a nickname for a road that twisted through Karasu. Businesses lined it, then built over it, then built over that, until the road became a stack. Each level is a full street of stalls, bars, clinics and rooms, carried on girders over the one below and joined by stairs and lifts. Newcomers stop and stare; it should not stand up. Levels are counted from the bottom. The higher you go, the cleaner, quieter and more expensive it gets, but this is still Karasu, and the top of the Ribbon is classy only by Karasu standards. The lowest levels barely see daylight. The stack winds down out of Old Town and levels out into the Strand.

76.content: The Ridge Families are the old-money dynasties of Cloudridge. They were wealthy before the corps rose, and they have survived by owning a piece of all of them: shares, debt, land and marriages. Few Ridge names appear on corporate boards, but most boards answer to Ridge money somewhere. The Families compete with each other through feuds, marriages and inheritance fights that can run for generations, and they close ranks against newcomers, especially the corporate rich of Helios Towers. They hire Aegis to guard their gates, fixers to handle their scandals, and runners to watch each other. They consider themselves the true owners of Lowlight, and on paper they very often are.

77.content: The Spine is a superhighway raised on enormous pylons. It cuts through the center of Lowlight, from Iron Reach past Nexus to Karasu and down toward the Marsh. It was built in the late 1900s, when the sea was taking ground and the city had to stack its roads to save space. It stands taller than nearly everything outside Helios Towers and Nexus. It counts as a district because people live in it: habs are built into the pylons and hung beneath the decks, whole neighborhoods in the dark under the road. Above them the traffic never stops. Rents are low and so is the ceiling. Residents call themselves Spiners and say they can tell the time by the sound of the freight.

78.content: The Strip-Miners are Lowlight's mercenary runners. They strip lacquer for anyone who pays: corps hitting other corps, fixers, gangs, people trying to erase a debt. They work in crews, with each runner specializing in one layer of defense, and they split every take by contract. They have no politics and say so; a Strip-Miner who worked for Cortex last week may hit Cortex this week. Their reputation rests on two things: they finish the job, and they never talk about it afterward. They meet in the dark and take most of their work through the Switchboard. The Capers hunt them more than any other clan, and every Strip-Miner knows someone who was caught and never seen again.

79.content: The Sump-Rats are the boat crews of the Marsh. They know every flooded street, collapsed floor and underwater passage, and they claim salvage on anything the water gives up: old machines, lost cargo, bodies. They run ferries across the Marsh for a fee, smuggle goods in through canals no patrol will follow, and charge outsiders to pass. Members mark their boats and their skin with tide lines. They are poor, tough and loyal to each other, and they hate the corps that abandoned the Marsh. Most of them are not cruel, but they are territorial, and people who try to work the water without them tend to be found in it. They trade with the Drowned Choir but don't trust it.

80.content: The Switchboard is the loose network of fixers who connect Lowlight's factions. A Switchboard fixer can find a runner, a crew, a smuggler, a doctor or a buyer for almost anything, and takes a cut for the introduction. There is no leader and no headquarters, only a web of people who vouch for each other, pass work along, and keep a strict code: never work both sides of the same job, never name a client, never sell out another fixer. Anyone who breaks the code is cut off, which in Lowlight is often fatal. The Switchboard deals with corps, gangs and clans alike and belongs to none of them. Most of the work done in the city's shadows passes through it at some point.

81.content: The Tilt is a bar down the Ribbon from Hae's, in a building that settled years ago, so the whole floor runs downhill toward the back wall. The owners never leveled it. The stools are bolted down, the glasses are heavy-bottomed, and the sign over the bar is a tipped glass in orange neon, as a warning. It has a long bar under hanging lamps, shelves of cheap bottles, a row of taps, worn red leather booths along one side, an old arcade cabinet that still takes coins, and a window full of Ribbon towers. The drinks are cheap and the music stays low enough to talk. Couriers, shift workers and people who don't explain why they're awake at three drink here. Workers from three different houses come in after shift and keep to their own tables. There is a rule against settling business inside, and the staff enforces it at the door. Cass works the late shift behind the bar. She pours, she teases, and she remembers everything said in front of her.

82.content: The Waterkeepers are the crews of Drownworks, organized into a tight brotherhood that runs the city's water reclamation. Officially they are a workers' guild. In practice they are one of the most respected and most dangerous groups in Lowlight, because they control something every person in the city needs every day. They guard the settling bays, pump houses and mains themselves, and they treat any threat to the water as an act of war. They take no bribes, make no deals with Scoma or the Sump-Rats, and keep the corps at arm's length. The Waterkeepers have gone on strike only twice. Both times the city stopped, and the corps gave in within days. Being called clean water by a Waterkeeper is high praise.

83.content: The Wheel-Men run the Strand. They control the fairground games, the pickpockets, the ticket scalping, and the protection money every stall on the boardwalk pays. Their leaders work in plain sight as ride operators, game hosts and barkers. They also control who gets into the Low Roller's cars, which means they control the most private meeting place on the Strand. They sell that privacy and keep an ear on what is said in it. The Wheel-Men prefer cons to violence and smiles to threats, but they have muscle when they need it. They protect the Scoma dealers on the boardwalk and take a cut of every sale. Corp security leaves them alone, because the Wheel-Men keep the Strand calm enough for tourists.

84.content: Silas and Ember Zhou are twins in their mid-twenties who share a two-room place on Level 2 of the Ribbon and work with Hicks's crew. Ember, the older by eleven minutes, is a punk netrunner with a spiky pixie cut streaked pink, teal and violet, a chrome implant on her right temple, piercings and tattoos, a Fairy Dust shirt and a denim jacket tied at her waist. Her handle is Spark, she is friendly and funny with everyone, and she is the best runner on the crew. Silas is tall, lanky and serious, with long messy hair and taped wire glasses. He works part time behind the counter at Second Socket on Level 4, watches its JOBS board, keeps the crew's gear running, and goes by Gumshoe on the grid. He watches old detective holovids and always wants to talk about the latest tech. They grew up downstack at their mother's deck-repair stall.

85.content: Tidal Isle sits in the bay as the city's front door. Every ship and passenger arriving in Lowlight clears customs here, and every immigrant is processed here, in long halls of booths, scanners and waiting benches. Getting through can take an hour or a year, depending on papers, sol and luck. Some people never get past the Isle. They live in the holding blocks and work the piers while their cases sit on someone's screen. Smugglers, fixers and forgers all keep business on the Isle, because the easiest way into Lowlight is through the front door with someone holding it open. The northwest corner belongs to the QDF, and new arrivals learn quickly not to look at it for long.

86.content: Titan is a corp in slow collapse, which makes it dangerous. Its mining fleets are gone and its import business shrinks every year, but it still owns land, warehouses, old debts and a great deal of hard sol. Titan's board is at war with itself. Different factions inside the company hire different crews, runners and fixers, sometimes against each other. Titan pays better than anyone for risky work because it has to: few people want to be tied to a company that may not exist next year. It is rumored to be quietly selling off assets, including orbital hardware nobody knew was still up there. Everyone in Nexus is waiting to see who picks over Titan's carcass, and Titan has no intention of dying quietly.

87.content: Titan began in ore extraction and staked its future on asteroid mining. When space flight was largely abandoned in the 2050s because of fuel costs, that bet failed, and Titan has been declining ever since. It is still a big name. It remains a major importer, its old wealth is enormous, and it holds land, debt and grudges all over the city. Its Nexus offices are far too big for the staff it has left. Titan's people talk about orbit the way old soldiers talk about a war, and a failing corp with that much money and nothing to lose makes everyone nervous.

88.content: True-North is a clan of ghosts devoted to the truth. They copy Spectra broadcasts, corporate filings and city records before those can be rewritten, and they keep the originals in hidden archives scattered across the grid and on paper. They leak what they find, often through Dead Air, and they never sell it. Anyone can try to reach them to ask for the real version of an event, but True-North decides who gets an answer. Nobody knows how many of them there are. Spectra calls them terrorists and pays the Capers to find them. To many people in Lowlight, True-North is the only reason anyone remembers what actually happened.

89.content: Velvet is Lowlight's red-light quarter, north of the Strand at the foot of the cliffs of Mirage Heights. Clubs, lounges, bathhouses and rooms rented by the hour fill its streets, and most of the workers are placed by houses that take a cut and hold their pay. On the cliff face above it sits a giant neon cat, visible across the city and plainly from Cloudridge. The Cat lights at dusk, which is why people say the Cat's up when night begins. The Cat glows directly beneath the Shelf, so Lowlight's government works every day above the brightest sign in the red-light quarter, and the city finds this very funny. Velvet is cleaner and quieter than outsiders expect. What it sells most is discretion.

90.content: Voltaic Logistics holds power through movement. Its manifests show what enters and leaves Lowlight, where it goes and who paid for it, and Voltaic sells that knowledge carefully. It automated most of its workforce years ago and is still fighting the last human crews in Dockside, whom it sees as both a cost and a security risk. Voltaic tolerates theft as long as it stays predictable; it budgets for the Freight Runners the way other companies budget for rain. When theft stops being predictable, Voltaic hires Aegis. A delayed shipment can bankrupt a small business, and Voltaic delays shipments when it wants something. Anyone who controls a choke point in the city, whether a bridge, a rail line or a pier, eventually gets a visit from Voltaic.

91.content: Voltaic Logistics moves everything in Lowlight that is not a person, and some things that are. It owns the automated shipping fleets in the bay, the sky-freighters overhead, the magnetic hyper-trains that carry freight through the city, and most of the cranes in Dockside and Iron Reach. If a crane is working, it is Voltaic's. Voltaic replaced most of its human workers years ago and keeps the rest on short contracts. Everything that crosses the city passes through Voltaic's systems at some point, which makes its manifests worth a great deal to runners.

92.content: Vrana is a grey river port across the water, all tenements, cranes and dry docks along a slow brown river. It built ships for a century, until the yards were automated and most of the welders and riveters were let go in a single season. Vranans have been coming to Lowlight ever since, most of them through Tidal Isle and many through the Ferrymen, because a Vranan trade card counts for little at customs. In Lowlight they are known as steady, blunt workers who fix things nobody else will touch, and who never quite stop talking about the yards. Older Vranans keep to Dockside and the lower Ribbon, where the cranes at least look familiar. The name means crow, which Karasu people find either funny or a good omen, depending on the night.
